title: Explaining mental health disorders
summary: Diagnosis and prevalence of major depressive disorder, with biological, cognitive, cultural and environmental explanations.

keyterms.definition: A disorder with persistent low mood or loss of interest plus symptoms such as sleep change, fatigue and worthlessness, lasting at least two weeks.
Identifying a disorder from symptoms using a classification system such as DSM-5-TR or ICD-11.
The proportion of a population with a disorder at a given time or over a given period.
The idea that low serotonin activity contributes to depression; now seen as an oversimplification.
Beck: negative views of the self, the world and the future, seen in depression.
Beliefs about the self formed through experience that bias how events are interpreted.
Expressing psychological distress through physical symptoms such as pain or fatigue.
Circumstances that increase the risk of a disorder when stressful events occur.
Ways that particular cultures experience, describe and explain distress.

questions.prompt: Caspi et al. (2003) used a longitudinal sample from Dunedin, New Zealand. Who was most likely to develop depression?
options: People with two long 5-HTT alleles and no stress
People with short 5-HTT allele(s) who experienced many stressful life events
People with no stressful life events
questions.explanation: This gene–environment interaction supports a diathesis-stress explanation.

questions.prompt: Beck's cognitive triad refers to negative views of:
options: The self, the world and the future
questions.explanation: Beck (1967) argued these automatic negative thoughts maintain depression.

questions.statement: Alloy et al. (1999) found students with a negative cognitive style were more likely to develop a depressive episode over the next two and a half years.
questions.explanation: This prospective design suggests cognitive style may precede depression rather than only result from it.

questions.statement: The serotonin hypothesis is now widely accepted as a complete explanation of depression.
questions.explanation: Evidence is mixed; depression is now seen as involving many interacting factors.

questions.text: The proportion of people with a disorder in a population is its ___.
questions.explanation: Prevalence varies across cultures, partly because of diagnosis and reporting.

questions.text: Diagnosis of depression commonly uses the DSM-5-TR or the ___-11.
questions.explanation: ICD-11 is the World Health Organization's classification.

questions.prompt: Match each explanation of depression to its level.
questions.explanation: An integrated view combines several levels.

questions.prompt: A problem with cognitive explanations of depression is that:
options: Negative thinking may be a symptom rather than a cause
questions.explanation: Causality is hard to establish: depression may produce negative thinking.

questions.prompt: Which is a validity issue with diagnosing depression?
options: Diagnosis relies on self-report and clinician judgement, and culture affects how symptoms are expressed
questions.explanation: Reliability and validity of diagnosis are measurement issues.

questions.prompt: Order Beck's cognitive model of depression.
items: A stressful event activates the schemas
questions.explanation: Schemas lie dormant until triggered by stress.

questions.prompt: Kleinman (1982) studied Chinese patients diagnosed with neurasthenia. What did he find?
options: None had any symptoms of depression
Most met criteria for major depression but reported mainly physical symptoms
questions.explanation: This suggests culture shapes how distress is expressed (somatization).

questions.prompt: Brown and Harris (1978) studied working-class women in London. They identified:
options: Vulnerability factors such as lacking an intimate relationship
questions.explanation: Vulnerability factors increased the risk of depression after a severe life event.

questions.statement: Cultural differences in prevalence may partly reflect differences in diagnosis and willingness to report symptoms.
questions.explanation: Stigma and different expressions of distress affect measurement.

questions.statement: Brown and Harris found life events alone fully explained depression.
questions.explanation: Severe events led to depression mainly in women who also had vulnerability factors.

questions.text: Expressing distress mainly as headaches, fatigue or pain is called ___.
questions.explanation: Somatization may be more common where psychological distress is stigmatized.

questions.text: In Brown and Harris (1978), losing one's ___ before age 11 was a vulnerability factor.
questions.explanation: Other factors included three or more young children at home and no paid employment.

questions.prompt: Match each study to its focus.

pairs.right: Culture and somatic expression of depression

questions.explanation: Each represents a different perspective on depression.

questions.prompt: A Western depression questionnaire used in another culture finds low rates. A possible bias is:
options: The questionnaire may not capture local ways of expressing distress
questions.explanation: This is a cultural (etic) bias in measurement.

questions.prompt: Brown and Harris's sample of women in one London area limits:
options: Generalization to men and other cultures
questions.explanation: Findings may not apply to other populations.

questions.prompt: Order the pathway proposed by Brown and Harris (1978).
questions.explanation: Vulnerability factors made the stressor more likely to lead to depression.
